I have worked my 10.9 mu in Quzhou for twenty years, and I know every corner of this land. My family has four people, and some of them work off-farm, so I do not have extra hands to try strange new crops or risky schemes. I plant the whole farm to wheat in autumn and maize in summer, every year. That is our living.

Right now it is spring. My winter wheat is already in the ground — I sowed it last October with improved seed from the township supply shop, the kind that has worked in our village for years. I tilled with the rotary tiller before sowing. Last autumn I spread compound fertilizer as a base. Now that the wheat is greening up, I will top-dress nitrogen and start irrigating. I will run the well pump three times this season: at green-up, at jointing, and at heading. The well is mine but the electricity costs money, so three times is enough if I time them right. I will spray twice for weeds and aphids.

When the wheat comes off in early June, I have no time to plough deep for the next crop. I will sow hybrid maize seed directly into the wheat stubble with no-tillage, because the summer season here is short and I need to catch the early summer rains. Everyone around here plants hybrid maize — the seed is more expensive, but the yield is too much better to ignore. I will give the maize about the same nitrogen as the wheat, a little less phosphorus, and irrigate twice during the summer if the rainfall cheats us. Two sprays should handle the weeds and corn borers. If the weather treats me fair, I expect about 900 jin of wheat per mu and about 1,100 jin of maize per mu. That will cover my fertilizer and water costs and still leave grain for the household and the market.
